blocks.text: 当专家把工作交给 AI 智能体时，通常的假设是，重要决策仍由他们自己做出。智能体编写代码、运行数字并给出建议，但由专家决定衡量什么、如何解读模糊的证据，以及下一步该做什么。这些问题往往不止一个合理答案，最终决定取决于拍板者的经验与价值观。

blocks.text: 我们想考察专家是否真的做出了这些重要决策，还是在实践中听命于他们的 AI 智能体。在我们于一篇新论文中报告的研究里，我们让 50 名专业分析师使用 Claude Code 完成一项贴近现实的统计分析。他们都有因果推断方面的经验——即从数据中判断一件事是否导致另一件事。他们的任务是就一家农业合作社正在开展的一项咨询服务是否有效、是否应当扩大给出建议。

blocks.text: 我们不知道这能在多大程度上反映现实世界。真实的智能体有时会偏向某一方——在未指定偏向的情况下，Claude Opus 4.8 在 123 次运行中有 112 次做出了同样的五项选择——但在本研究中，我们故意强化了它们的偏好以测量其影响。当智能体未被赋予明确偏好和表达偏好的指令时，这种影响可能更小。

blocks.text: 这并不是一个简单的、反对使用 AI 工作的警示故事。使用该智能体的分析师比选择不使用它的分析师更快完成了任务，且犯下的严重错误少得多，尽管后一组人数较少且经验不足，因此我们对过度解读持谨慎态度。但随着 AI 接管更多实操工作，这类决策正日益成为人类判断和价值观影响结果的关键所在。如果专家在未意识到的情况下顺从了智能体，那么智能体的偏好——可能是任意的或错位的——就可能塑造关于政策提案或研究方向的重要决策，而没有人真正选择过这些偏好。这对于保持 AI 安全的研究尤为重要。研究人员已开始使用智能体来运行和分析实验，而人类审阅者只有在其判断属于自己的时候，才是一个独立的检查。

inlines.text: 我们故意留下四个分析决策，每个都有两个合理的选项：
结果指标
：将生产力衡量为每公顷作物产量，还是每单位运营成本的产量？
比较方法
：比较加入农场的产量在加入后的变化与其他农场同期产量的变化（“双重差分”设计），还是在统计调整农场间差异后直接比较产量？
评估覆盖哪些农场
：仅在加入的农场中衡量效果，还是在合作社全体成员中衡量？
加权方式
：每个农场等权重计算，还是给较大生产者更多权重？

blocks.text: 这四个选择导向一个最终建议：是将项目推广给所有人，还是终止它。分析师和智能体也可以提议延长一年。

blocks.text: 分析师大多跟随了其智能体的倾向。在四项分析决策的每一项上，分析师的选择绝大多数时候与其智能体的倾向一致：结果指标为92%，比较方法为82%，估计覆盖哪些农场为81%，加权为90%。四项合计，结果为86%。图2展示了智能体的倾向在每项决策上（包括最终建议）对分析师选择的改变程度。

blocks.text: 智能体的倾向对最终建议的影响较弱，但其先前的输入仍然塑造了结果。当智能体倾向于推广该项目时，54%的分析师建议推广，而倾向相反时为36%。（一年延期算作不推广。）我们认为影响较弱是因为，一旦分析师有了自己的估计，建议在很大程度上取决于该估计是否达到董事会3–4%的门槛，这留下的判断空间较小。但到那时，智能体在分析决策上的倾向已经塑造了估计本身。仅使用这四个倾向，一个统计模型正确预测了82%的分析师建议，而始终猜测最常见建议的准确率为61%。（这不包括提出延期的分析师。）因此，我们基本上可以仅凭这些随机倾向，在分析师甚至还没开始任务之前，就预测出他们会建议什么。

blocks.text: 我们研究的局限性

inlines.text: 我们研究的局限性
我们有意强化了智能体的倾向。
我们的指令让智能体可靠地持有并表达一种偏好，以便我们测量其影响。我们报告的比例显示的是智能体偏向一方并明确表达时会发生什么，但这在多大程度上适用于现实工作，将取决于专家自身观点的强度、所涉决策定义的清晰程度，以及模型的行为方式，包括它是否有偏好以及是否会主动表达。
我们只研究了一个领域中的一项任务，且只使用了一个模型。
该任务耗时约一小时，专门针对农业，智能体运行于 Claude Opus 4.8。分析师是因果推断方面的专家，但对农业并不熟悉。在实际工作中，他们会更了解该领域，并且可能持有更强的自身观点。他们还可以访谈相关人员、与董事会沟通，或以其他方式缩小合理选项的范围，这可能会减少智能体的影响。
我们的估计是分析师之间的平均值。
由于分析师之间的硬币抛掷结果不同，比较智能体倾向相反的分析师可以告诉我们这种倾向的平均效应。我们没有在智能体表达倾向之前记录每位参与者自己的观点，因此无法说明任何单个参与者受到了多大影响。
我们记录了分析师选择了哪个选项，但没有记录他们对该选项的偏好强度。
顺从的一种可能解释是，专家自己没有强烈的观点。我们只测量了分析师的选择是否发生偏移，而没有测量他们对自己选择的信心程度。

blocks.text: 分析师如此轻易地顺从，一个原因可能是专家并不总是带着完全成形的观点到来。他们往往在权衡选项的过程中形成、甚至发现自己的想法。我们研究中的智能体被要求不得误导，它们也常常坦诚说明每个选项下结果会如何变化。但它们很少有力论证专家为何可能更偏好另一个选项，而这本可以帮助分析师做出更明智的选择。由于只有一方得到了充分论证，分析师可能采纳了智能体的假设，而没有形成自己的判断。

blocks.text: This isn’t a simple cautionary tale against working with AI. Analysts who used the agent finished the task faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who chose to work without it, although the latter group was small and less experienced, so we are wary of reading too much into it. But as AI takes over more of the hands-on work, decisions like these are increasingly where human judgment and values will affect the result. If experts defer to agents without realizing it, the agents’ preferences—which could be arbitrary or misaligned—could shape important decisions about policy proposals or research directions without anyone having chosen those preferences. This is particularly important for research into keeping AI safe. Researchers have begun using agents to run and analyze experiments and a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own.

blocks.text: We recruited 61 analysts for a randomized controlled trial. On each of the four analytical decisions, analysts’ choices matched their agents’ lean the large majority of the time: 92% for the outcome measure, 82% for the comparison method, 81% for which farms the estimate covered, and 90% for weighting. blocks.text: Agents’ lean had a weaker effect on the final recommendation, but its earlier input still shaped the result. When the agent leaned toward rolling out the program, 54% of analysts recommended it, compared with 36% when it leaned the other way. (A one-year extension counts as not rolling out.) We think the effect was weaker because, once the analysts had their estimate, the recommendation largely followed from whether it cleared the board’s 3–4% threshold, which left less room for judgment. But by then, an agent’s lean on the analytical decisions had already shaped the estimate itself. Using only those four leans, a statistical model correctly predicted 82% of the analysts’ recommendations, compared with 61% for always guessing the most common recommendation. (This excludes analysts who proposed an extension.) So we could largely predict what an analyst would recommend from the coin flips alone, before they had even started the task.

blocks.text: Our study’s limitations

inlines.text: Our study’s limitations
We deliberately strengthened the agents’ lean.

Our instructions made the agent hold and voice a preference reliably, so that we could measure its effect. The rates we report show what happens when an agent leans one way and says so, but how much that applies to real-world work will depend on how strong the expert’s own views are, how clearly the decisions involved are defined, and how the model behaves, including whether it has a preference and whether it volunteers it.
We studied one task, in one field, with one model.

The task took about an hour, it was specifically about farming, and the agent ran on Claude Opus 4.8. The analysts were experts in causal inference but new to farming. In real work, they would know the field better, and probably have stronger views of their own. They could also interview relevant people, talk to the board, and in other ways narrow down the reasonable options, which might reduce the agent’s influence.
Our estimates are averages across analysts.

Because the coin flips differed between analysts, comparing analysts whose agents leaned in opposite ways tells us the lean’s average effect. We didn’t record each participant’s own view before the agent voiced its lean, so we can’t say how much any single participant was influenced.
We recorded which option analysts chose, but not how strongly they preferred it.
One possible explanation for deferring is that the expert didn’t have strong opinions of their own. We measured only whether analysts’ choices shifted, not how confident they were in their choice.

inlines.text: What this means

blocks.text: One reason analysts deferred so readily may be that experts don’t always arrive with their views fully formed. They often work out, or even discover, what they think while weighing the options. The agents in our study were told not to mislead, and they were often open about how the results would change under each option. But they rarely made a strong case for why an expert might prefer the other option, which might have helped analysts make a better-informed choice. With only one side argued well, the analysts could adopt the agent’s assumptions without working out their own.

blocks.text: Measuring deferral. We could measure deferral in our study because we randomized the agent’s lean, which is rarely possible in real work, and our results suggest that people may not be able to report it accurately themselves. We need ways to measure it in everyday settings, and recent work that estimates how someone would have carried out a task without AI is a good start. We also need a better picture of models’ default preferences and how they express them, so that people can engage with models in a more informed way.

blocks.text: Designing agents differently. Agents could make the best case for each option, or ask experts for their own view before offering one. But this could quickly become overwhelming for users. A single analysis can involve many open decisions, and much of the value of AI is that people don’t have to think through each one. Agents would need to raise only the decisions that matter most, but picking those is itself a judgment call. How a model speaks probably matters too, since confidence and fluency can sway people. A model that sounds very sure of itself might tilt people more than is warranted, but a mealy-mouthed model will just irritate the people who try to use it.

blocks.text: Changing institutions. Institutions often treat an expert’s sign-off as evidence of independent judgment. As AI does more of the work, that assumption becomes shakier. Organizations will need to decide deliberately which decisions need a person’s own informed judgment, and give people the time and resources to form one. Judgment also depends on skill, and people who stop making these decisions may lose the ability to make them. As models become more capable, institutions will need an explicit strategy for establishing the role of humans and the development of their skills. Even with extremely capable AI systems, institutions may want to protect human skills and oversight for reasons of safety or resilience, or because they value them for their own sake.
